query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an ultrathin, engineered oxide buffering layer onto the surface of high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles during colloidal synthesis will enhance their structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic, multi-element HEA nanoparticles synthesized via a colloidal solvothermal method, exhibiting a homogeneous solid‐solution structure without surface modification.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled ultrathin oxide coating during synthesis, serving as a buffering layer on nanoparticle surfaces.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environments typical for catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K), under both inert and low-oxygen atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous, ultrathin oxide buffering layer.
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer acts as a physical barrier that suppresses surface atomic diffusion and sintering, thereby reducing elemental segregation and phase instability during high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated HEA nanoparticles will show significantly lower rates of sintering, maintain a more uniform elemental distribution, and exhibit enhanced phase stability compared to non-coated nanoparticles under identical thermal conditions.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles prepared without the oxide coating, which are expected to show increased sintering and chemical segregation under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is contingent on maintaining an optimal coating thickness and uniformity; extreme thermal cycling or deviations in coating composition may diminish the stabilization effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal thickness and material composition of the oxide layer and its long-term behavior under cyclic thermal stresses remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles using the colloidal synthesis method. Apply an ultrathin oxide buffering layer to one set while leaving the other set uncoated. Expose both sets to high-temperature conditions mimicking catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operating environments for extended periods. Compare the structural integrity and compositional uniformity of both sets using high-resolution microscopy and elemental analysis.
measurements: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to assess sintering and particle size evolution
Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to evaluate elemental segregation
X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) to monitor phase stability
Performance tests related to catalytic or thermoelectric efficiency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxide-coated HEA nanoparticles do not show a statistically significant reduction in sintering, elemental segregation, and phase degradation relative to the uncoated nanoparticles under the test conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Since the successful fabrication of the first-ever entropy- stabilized oxides, or, more general, high-entropy oxides (HEOs), such solid solutions have drawn much attention due to their unique compositional and structural features, namely, the extreme chemical disorder incorporated into single-crystal structures (). One representative example is that the metal ions in (Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)O are unanimously divalent and randomly occupy the cationic sites in a rocksalt structure. These cations are coordinated by lattice oxygen in an octahedral configuration, even though Cu(II) and Zn(II) are usually four coordinated to oxygen atoms as, for example, in their binary oxides (). This stabilization of Cu(II) and Zn(II) in an unfavorable configuration is ascribable to the increased configurational entropy and a high solid solution temperature (, , ). Inspired by rocksalt HEOs, researchers have undertaken extensive work to develop diverse types of HEOs. In nanomaterial science, developing methods for the rapid and reliable synthesis of nanoparticles, especially from complex materials like HEAs, is essential [,]. HEAs, with their composition of four or more principal elements in nearly equal molar ratios, have significantly altered the traditional approach to alloy design. These alloys are distinguished by their diverse multi-element composition, leading to an array of desirable physicochemical and mechanical properties [,]. Their versatile application potential spans a range of industries, including high-temperature materials, anti-corrosion, electrocatalysis, advanced welding, and brazing [,,,,]. The real power of HEAs lies in their high-entropy effect, which promotes the formation of simple solid phases over a more intermetallic composition, thereby granting these alloys remarkable characteristics. In our study, we selected an HEA composed of CuCoMn1.75NiFe0.25 due to its potential catalytic properties stemming from its composition, its effectiveness in brazing and welding applications, and the high probability of being single phase [,,,,,]. reading.lever: Integrate a controlled, ultrathin oxide buffering (coating) layer during colloidal synthesis to stabilize HEA nanoparticle surfaces at high temperatures.
reading.why: By combining a robust colloidal solvothermal synthesis with an engineered oxide surface layer (inspired by HEO buffering), we can target high-temperature structural stability while maintaining low noble-metal content.
